sections.text:
1 Post hoc verbum in margine codicis Veneti prima manus adiecit : [Κ]αὶ τὴν
ἶβιν καὶ τὸν κέρκοπα (sic) Αἰγυπτίοις ἔνθεν ἐδόκει τιμᾶν· ἀμφότερα γὰρ τὰ ζῷα
σελήνῃ συμπαθῆ εἶναι προσείκασται· ἡ μὲν ἶβις αὐτῷ τῷ σχήματι ἐμφερὴς τὰ ἄκρα
μὲν ὀμιχλαίνουσα, λευκαίνουσα δὲ τὰ μέσα, καθάπερ ἡ αἰθρία· ὅτε γὰρ ὁ οὐρανὸς
ἀσέληνος οὐδὲ ἴβιδες ὁρῶσι, μύουσι δὲ τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς τοῦτον τὸν χρόνον καὶ
ἄσιτοι ἐγκαρτεροῦσι τὸ συγγενὲς στοιχεῖον ἀναμένουσαι· ὁ δὲ κέρκοψ (sic) δηλο-
τέρας ἔχει τὰς ἐνεργείας· ὅτε γὰρ αὔξει ἡ σελήνη ὁ τῶν ὀφθάλμων κύκλος αὐτοῦ
εὐρύνεται, ὅτε δὲ μειοῦται, τὸ τῶν ὀμμάτων περιφερὲς συστέλλεται· Δέρκυλλος
δέ φησιν ὅτι γεννᾶται ἐν τῷ Ὑδάσπῃ ποταμῷ λίθος λυχνήτης (sic) καλούμενος.
οὗτος Σελήνης αὐξομένης ἦχον μελῳδίας ἀποδίδωσι καὶ ἐν Ἄρ.ρει (sic) δὲ τῷ
ποταμῷ τῆς Κελτικῆς τίκτεται ἰχθύς, κλωπίων (sic) αὐτὸν οἱ ἐπιχώριοι καλοῦσι, ὃς
αὐξομένης σελήνης λευκὸς γίνεται, μειούσης δὲ μελαίνεται = Lydus, De Mens.,
III, 11, p, 51, 5 ss., Wünsch. Quae tamen non ex ipso Lydi thesauro deprompsisse
videtur librarius sed ex Anastasio Sinaïta, qui in Hexaemero Lydum expilavit; cf.
Migne, Patr. gr., t. 89, col. 904 [875].
2 Haec et alia quae cursu lunae efficiuntur, describit quoque Apomasar, III, 13,
Περὶ τῶν ἐνεργειῶν τῆς Σελήνης, cf. supra cod. 2, f. 70v.
sections.en:
1 After this word in the margin of the Venetian codex the first hand added: And the
ibis and the cercopithecus (sic) seemed to the Egyptians to be honored from this; for both animals
are likened to be sympathetic to the moon; the ibis being similar to it in shape, darkening the extremities
but whitening the middle, just like the clear sky; for when the sky is
moonless neither do ibises see, but they close their eyes during this time and
endure without food waiting for the kindred element; and the cercopithecus (sic) has clearer
activities; for when the moon waxes the circle of its eyes
widens, but when it wanes, the circumference of the eyes contracts; and Dercyllus
says that in the river Hydaspes a stone called lychnites (sic) is produced.
This, when the Moon is waxing, gives off a sound of melody, and in the river Arar (sic)
of Celtica a fish is born, the locals call it clopion (sic), which
when the moon is waxing becomes white, but when it is waning becomes black = Lydus, De Mens.,
III, 11, p, 51, 5 ss., Wünsch. Which however the scribe seems not to have drawn from the treasury of Lydus himself
but from Anastasius of Sinai, who in the Hexaemeron pillaged Lydus; cf.
Migne, Patr. gr., t. 89, col. 904 [875].
2 These and other things which are brought about by the course of the moon, Apomasar also describes, III, 13,
On the activities of the Moon, cf. above cod. 2, f. 70v.

summary.headline: Lunar Sympathy and Stellar Influences
summary.text: Discussion of lunar and stellar sympathy: the Moon’s waxing and waning affect animal organs, shellfish, winds, seas, rivers, corpses, and the surrounding environment, supporting the claim that stellar mixtures pre-signify bodily qualities and future events. Marginal material cites Dercyllus, John Lydus, Anastasius of Sinai, and Apomasar on lunar phenomena.
